newsitem.title: USA: DC panel urges US takeover of some city programs.
newsitem.headline: DC panel urges US takeover of some city programs.

text.p: The District of Columbia financial control board called on the U.S. government to fund up to $1 billion annually of non-municipal functions currently paid for by the financially strapped District of Columbia, including Medicaid, prisons, mental health, roads and other infrastructure.

"Plain and simple, we need to fundamentally redefine the relationship between the federal and District governments," Stephen Harlan, vice chairman of the control board, said at a press briefing to release the board's "strategic plan" for the financially troubled city.
Reuters reported the key points of the 26-page strategic plan Wednesday.

Harlan said, "If we do not reach a workable solution together, we run the risk that the District will become a complete financial ward of the federal government. We are faced with a city that is not viable in the long-term under its current structure."

Harlan said the notion that the control board is recommending "giveaways" to the District is wrong. He said the federal-District relationship created in 1974 when the city was granted Home Rule has "been from the start one-sided."
Control board chair Andrew Brimmer said the plan is "our road map out of the District's crisis and into the future."
He said the 1974 Home Rule pact "fell far short" of a balanced transfer of financial resources from Congress to the city.
Parry Young, director of public finance for Standard & Poor's Ratings Group, called the board's report "encouraging."
"A lot of the issues are issues we've talked about for years. But the fact that the board has established timetables and plans for dealing with these problems is encouraging," Young said.
The plan sets 31 deadlines for major city actions between now and October 1, 1998. By the end of January, for instance, the city and board will report on D.C.'s massive unfunded pension liability.

By March 31, the city must make recommendations on what to do about the current federal contribution to city funding and the city's troubled financial management system. Also by March 31, the city is to issue a 10-year "revenue projection," the board said.
By September 30, the city and board will report on the city's "infrastructure financing needs," the board said.
